thread.title: Stocks are looking kind of (gulp) cheap after jobs data, tax cuts - MarketWatch

author: Tim Mullaney
title: Stocks are looking kind of (gulp) cheap after jobs data, tax cuts - MarketWatch
text:
Thursday, it was the Dow Jones Industrial Average hitting 25,000 while payroll processor ADP reported that companies added 250,000 jobs in December. Friday it was the news from the Labor Department that the economy added 148,000 workers last month , and the unemployment rate stayed at 4.1% — the lowest of this expansion.
Something is picking up here, compared with even a few weeks ago, when I predicted the S&P 500 SPX, +0.38% would rise to just 2,730 this year — which happened on Jan. 4. But what is it? And why is it happening?
Some of the answers are boring and complicated (like the reasons for the gap between ADP’s jobs numbers and those of the Labor Department), but some are easy. After a year of Donald Trump claiming credit for market gains he didn’t cause — and job gains that are still 25% smaller than the monthly climbs in 2015, before he showed up — we may be at the beginning of gains he does cause.
The one thing we absolutely know a corporate tax cut like the one Trump signed last month will do is boost after-tax corporate earnings (even if it doesn’t boost pretax profit, sales or economic activity by a penny). Strategists across Wall Street are revising their 2018 earnings estimates upward to reflect the one positive thing we know the new tax law will accomplish.
The new law will add about 9% to corporate profits, BMO Capital Markets strategist Brian Belski says. Instead of projecting that companies in the S&P will earn $145 per share this year, indexed to each company’s weight in the S&P average, Belski now says corporate America will earn $158 a share.
Moody’s Analytics’ Mark Zandi estimates the tax bill will add 250,000 jobs in 2018. And if the economy is finding another gear independent of the direct impact of lower taxes -- as the job numbers suggest — the “bull case” has them earning $170 a share, Belski says. Similar numbers come from UBS strategist Keith Parker, who raised his 2018 S&P 500 target price to 3,150.
“The lowering of the corporate tax rate from 35% to 21% should provide a tailwind for earnings, which has already been growing at the highest clip since early 2012, according to our blended earnings growth model,” Belski wrote in a note to clients this week, sticking with his 2018 target of 2,950 for the S&P 500.
Read: Here’s what every S&P 500 company actually pays in taxes
At Belski’s aggressive earnings number of $170, my own 2018 target of 2,730 for the S&P works out to 16 times earnings — not expensive by historical standards. Even in his base-case earnings scenario, it’s 17 times. That means I’ve got to raise my numbers too; I picked 2,730 in late November assuming Trump would find some way not to get the tax bill through a Republican-controlled Senate.
But 16 times earnings is too low for an economy that seems to be gathering steam (notwithstanding Friday’s jobs number) and has the earnings crack of a deficit-financed corporate tax cut on its side. So put me down for a nice, round S&P 3,000 — and, as I said in November about 2,730, if I’m wrong it’s probably because I’m a little bit low.
Read: Tax cuts mean stock market ‘almost as cheap’ as a year ago: David Tepper
Tracking estimates have the economy growing at a 2.9% to 3.9% annual rate in the fourth quarter, depending on whether you believe Moody’s Analytics (the lower number) or the New York Federal Reserve Bank’s Nowcast. These numbers have their issues — they don’t, for example, do well at picking up inventory fluctuations that can make the gross domestic product growth numbers move up and down, and which accounted for about a quarter of the economy’s growth from July to September — but they all are higher than fourth-quarter forecasts from three months ago.
Now, Friday’s Labor Department report is close to the 164,000 average monthly gain for the prior 12 months. The pattern is still almost exactly the 160,000-job monthly gain economists began predicting in early 2016, reasoning that labor markets would cool down as full employment approached, paving the way for faster wage gains.
Read: While there are signs of supply-side issues in the jobs market, the December report may be more noise than signal
Economists like Moody’s Analytics’ Mark Zandi now say the unemployment rate is headed down to 3.5% or so, lower than it was even in the 1990s.
“We’re running out of bodies,” said Zandi, who estimated on a conference call Thursday that the tax bill will add 250,000 jobs in 2018. “The unemployment rate is going south. With deficit-financed tax cuts it’s going to be hard to derail that train.’’
We’ve all speculated all last year about whether prospects for the tax bill were boosting stocks, but now that the law is signed, things are more tangible. Trump had nothing to do with all-day breakfast at McDonalds (whose shares MCD, +0.06% are up 44% in the last year) besides eating it sometimes; he opposes changes in health-care delivery that have driven Dow component UnitedHealth Group UNH, +1.59% 38% higher, and he certainly didn’t invent the iPhone 8 or pull China’s economy from the abyss it confronted in 2015, which are the reasons Apple shares AAPL, +1.03% have surged 47%.
But he is the guy who cut corporate taxes. And that means shareholders get more of the pie right now, with individual taxpayers handling the interest payments on the $1.4 trillion the bill will add to deficits later. And that’s the best reason to trust that 2,730 isn’t the top for the S&P this year.
Give the devil his due, whether you consider that a figure of speech or not.
